title: Mobile phones in the spread of unreliable information on Twitter: evidence from the 2017 French presidential campaign
screen_reason: Observed platform data: 2,063,066 campaign tweets containing links whose linked source was classified reliable vs unreliable against the Décodex source-reliability database, reported as the share of shared links that are unreliable, split by device (Table 2) and by political community (Table 3a). That is a quantitative share of shared items carrying unreliable sources with a stated denominator, i.e. SHARING (content_share).

estimates.platform: Twitter (tweets/retweets posted from the Twitter mobile application, 'Mobile OS')
estimates.measure_type: % of link-carrying tweets/retweets posted from a mobile device whose linked information source was classified unreliable
estimates.denominator: 1,744,591 tweets/retweets posted from mobile operating systems that contained a link to an information source codeable for reliability, within a keyword corpus on the five main 2017 French presidential candidates
estimates.definition: the tweet's linked information source is listed as 'unreliable' (or hardly reliable) in the Décodex database of French-language news sources, complemented by the authors' manual coding of blogs and non-professional media
estimates.misinfo_def: "Décodex references the main French-language news sources and classifies them according to their reliability. It identifies and distinguishes reliable sources, which carry out the real journalistic work of verification, from those that are unreliable or hardly reliable, [page break in the original] and which are known to have relayed misinformation or disinformation in the past."
estimates.page_loc: p. 12, Table 2 (Reliability of Sources Shared on Twitter According to Platform), Mobile OS row
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Décodex, the source-reliability database built by journalists of Le Monde (domain names classified reliable vs unreliable/hardly reliable), complemented by the authors' own manual classification of sources absent from Décodex (party sites, NGOs, blogs, non-professional media). No inter-coder reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: In determining such reliability, researchers typically use data from fact-checking sites and the thousands of examples of false information identified therein (Vosoughi et al., 2018). For our research we used the Décodex, a French database that was developed by reporters working for the daily newspaper Le Monde
estimates.notes: Device split (mobile app vs desktop web browser) is the paper's headline contrast, so both device rows are kept. denom_scope coded political_news because the denominator is links shared inside an election-campaign keyword corpus (candidate keywords/hashtags), not a single substantive issue. Unit is a tweet carrying at least one link; reliability attaches to the linked domain. Arithmetic note: the two device n's in Table 2 (1,744,591 + 564,741 = 2,309,332) exceed the 2,063,066 tweets the Method says were coded for reliability; the paper does not reconcile this, and no pooled overall unreliable share is reported anywhere.

estimates.moderator_quote: We classified them into two categories: 1) “Mobile OS” (Mobile Operating System) for Twitter used on mobile devices, and 2) “Non-Mobile OS” for Twitter used from a web browser on a computer.
estimates.notes: Same corpus and coding as the mobile row; this is the desktop comparison arm of the paper's headline device effect ("the portion of unreliable sources shared via the Twitter mobile application is higher by 4.55 percentage points").

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Table 3a gives the unreliable share by political community crossed with device: Mobile OS LFI 3.34% (n=203,765), PS 0.71% (71,764), REM 0.88% (89,053), LR 14.28% (250,987), FN 47.48% (230,440); Non-Mobile OS LFI 2.80% (190,356), PS 0.54% (97,567), REM 0.36% (179,463), LR 11.19% (465,766), FN 37.52% (283,905). These ten values are verbatim and the FN result is a headline claim of the abstract, but they are partisan subgroups of the two rows already extracted, so I kept the device-level rows only (R4, quality over quantity) and record the subgroup values here for an adjudicator. Note also that the table's n column is labelled against the 'Reliable' line only, so it is ambiguous whether n is the community total or the reliable count; the percentages within each device x community cell sum to 100%, which suggests n is the cell total. (2) 'During the 2017 campaign, the website [Fdesouche] represented 20.32% of the unreliable references in our corpus shared from a mobile phone' — a single named source's share of unreliable references. Not extracted as CONCENTRATION because R1 requires a group expressed as a % of sources and no such conc_group_pct is stated (one site out of an unstated total). (3) Figure 2/3 shares (press 78.44% mobile vs 89.59% web; social media 10.09%; content libraries 2.78% vs 0.82%) are source-TYPE shares, not falsity shares, and the unreliable complement would have to be computed, which R8 forbids. (4) 30.82% of tweets contained a URL and 46.99%/53.01% mobile/web splits are corpus-composition figures, not misinformation shares.

rob.design: Keyword/hashtag collection of 38,346,765 tweets from 2,163,812 accounts on the five main 2017 French presidential candidates (25 Nov 2016 - 12 May 2017); 13,044,619 link-carrying (re)tweets, of which 11,048,901 coded for source type and 2,063,066 for source reliability. Political communities identified by Louvain community detection on the mention/retweet graph plus qualitative expert labelling, with 22,853 profiles manually checked. Reliability coded from the Décodex domain list plus authors' manual complement; no inter-coder reliability statistic and no accuracy validation of Décodex reported; unreliability is source-level, not claim-level.
